text.p: Britain's high street banks remained cautious about leading supermarkets moving into financial services, but analysts said on Thursday competition was likely to be limited to niche products.
"I don't expect them to take over (from banks), but it could (reinforce) the trend for banks ensuring they make products accurately priced on their own merit," said John Leonard of Salomon Brothers.

Supermarket group J.Sainsbury Plc launched Sainsbury's Bank, its joint venture with Bank of Scotland , on Wednesday, offering an Instant Access account paying 5.75 percent annual interest, along with credit cards and other services to come.
Market leader Tesco Plc has switched its link from National Westminster to Royal Bank of Scotland, while supermarket chain Safeway has joined forces with Abbey National,

Neither of the Scottish banks have a strong presence outside their region, and analysts said Abbey National had a relatively weak presence outside London, so a link with well-known national brand names could give them a higher profile.

For the four major British high street banks -- National Westminster, Barclays Plc, Lloyd's TSB Group and Midland, part of HSBC Holdings, -- linking up with supermarkets risks lowering their profile or even subsuming their own brand names as well as raising competitive hackles.

National Westminster, which had run Tesco's ClubCard Plus account since its launch last summer, was clear that Tesco's plans for further financial services would have conflicted with its own strategy.
Barclays said earlier this week it had no plans for a supermarket tie-up.

"We are not looking at a partnership with any company that would use their brand name," personal sector director Richard Reay-Smith said when the company announced annual pre-tax profits of 2.36 billion pounds ($3.8 billion) on Tuesday.
But analysts said competition was likely to be in niche markets rather than across the broad spread of financial services which banks offer their customers.

"Areas of competition could emerge in current accounts and credit cards," said an analyst, "but I can't see shoppers burdened with the weekend's groceries sitting down for lengthy discussions on a mortgage."

Analysts said the 5.75 percent interest offered by Sainsbury's Bank was very attractive, but pointed out the market is skewed currently as customers of building societies heading for flotations hang on for share handouts.
Tesco is offering 5.5 percent interest and Safeway's comparable account gives five percent while Barclays Instant Savings offers 3.15 percent -- but only on balances of at least 10,000 pounds.
Analysts warned that such high rates from supermarket ventures might not be sustainable.
"It's easier to pay high rates when you don't have any savings," said Panmure Gordon's David Poutney.
Customers might be attracted by individual strong offers from the grocery bankers, analysts said, but were unlikely to switch all banking.
"It takes time, effort and money to change banks, we should never underestimate public inertia," an analyst said.
Nevertheless, the supermarkets seem confident these financial ventures will be profitable -- although expectations are well below the profits seen by Barclays.
Tesco said it expected profits in the second or third year of operation after a loss of five to 10 million pounds in the first year.

Marketing director Tim Mason said the group was eyeing similar profits from financial services to those achieved by retailer Marks & Spencer, which generated 61 million pounds last year after 15 years in the business.

"Supermarkets have good brands and they are trusted by customers. As long as they do financial services effectively and at a better rate, there will always be a place for their offer," an analyst said. ($ = 0.620 British Pounds)
